title: Design a Payment System
subtitle: Watch one card payment survive a timeout, a retry, a duplicate webhook and a bank mismatch without charging twice.
learn: How an idempotency key turns a retried payment request into a safe replay
Why a payment timeout means 'unknown', not 'failed'
How a double-entry ledger makes money movements auditable and self-checking
Why webhooks need dedup and why you cannot trust them alone
How reconciliation catches the errors every other layer missed
Why 'exactly-once' is really at-least-once plus idempotency

steps.title: Charge once, no matter what
steps.body: A customer taps Pay on a 50.00 order. The request leaves the phone, but the response gets lost in a tunnel. The app cannot tell whether the charge happened, so it sends the request again. Networks fail all the time, so retries are certain. The design question is how to make a retry harmless, because charging someone twice is the one bug a payment system must never ship.
steps.idea: In payments, retries are guaranteed, so the system must be safe under repetition by design.
steps.caption: The merchant app sends a payment, and may have to send it again.

steps.title: The idempotency key
steps.body: The client makes a random key (a UUID) once per purchase and sends it in a header on every attempt. This is the idempotency key: "idempotent" means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The API first inserts the key into a store with a unique constraint, saving a hash of the request body. Whoever inserts first owns the work. Later requests with the same key are not processed again; they get the saved outcome. The same key with a different body is rejected as a client bug. If the first attempt is still running, the duplicate waits or gets a 409 Conflict.
steps.idea: A unique-keyed insert before any side effect decides, atomically, who is allowed to do the work.
steps.caption: The API claims the key in a store before touching any money.

steps.title: Authorize with the PSP
steps.body: A payment service provider (PSP), such as a card processor, talks to the card networks and banks for us. The API records the payment as PENDING in the payments database, then calls the PSP. (The diagram draws the key store and payments database separately; if they share one database, the key claim and this record can be one transaction.) It also sends its own payment id as the PSP's idempotency key, so the PSP protects us the same way we protect the merchant. The PSP approves and returns an authorization id. We assume a one-step charge, with funds reaching the merchant days later.
steps.idea: Idempotency must hold at every hop: our API, and again on the call to the provider.
steps.caption: Happy path: the payment is recorded as pending, then approved by the PSP.

steps.title: The call times out
steps.body: Now replay it with the reply lost: the PSP charged the card, but its answer never reached us. After a 10 second timeout, the API cannot tell what happened. A timeout is not a failure; the money may have moved. So the API marks the payment UNKNOWN, keeps the key claimed, and does not ship the order or refund yet. Guessing "failed" here is how double charges and lost sales are born.
steps.idea: A timeout means 'unknown'. Treat unknown as its own state and resolve it by asking, never by guessing.
steps.caption: The PSP charged the card, but its reply is lost.

steps.title: The retry replays safely
steps.body: The client retries with the same key. The API finds the key already claimed and the payment UNKNOWN, so it does not make a second charge. It calls the PSP again with the same PSP idempotency key, and the PSP returns the original approval instead of charging twice. The API saves that result against the key, and every later retry gets it back instantly. The real charge count stays at one.
steps.idea: Retry with the same key is a question ('what happened?'), not a second command.
steps.caption: The same key at every step lets the PSP replay its first result.

steps.title: Double-entry ledger
steps.body: Once approved, the API writes the money movement to a ledger, a permanent record of every transaction. It is double-entry: each transaction has at least two rows that add up to zero. Here we debit the PSP receivable (money the PSP owes us) 50.00 and credit the merchant's payable 50.00, less a fee row if there is one. Ledger rows are never changed or deleted. A mistake is fixed by a new, opposite transaction. Because every transaction balances, total debits minus total credits must always be zero.
steps.idea: Double entry makes money conserved by construction, and any imbalance is instantly visible.
steps.caption: Two balanced rows are added in one database transaction.

steps.title: Webhooks report later outcomes
steps.body: The PSP also sends webhooks (messages it posts to our server) such as payment.succeeded, because some outcomes arrive later and responses can be lost. Our endpoint checks the PSP's signature, puts each event on a queue, and replies fast. A worker marks the payment CAPTURED. Delivery is at-least-once, so an event can arrive three times or out of order. So we save each event id under a unique constraint and apply the state change in the same database transaction.
steps.idea: Webhooks are at-least-once and unordered, so consume them with dedup by event id and state checks.
steps.caption: A duplicate webhook is absorbed, so the ledger changes only once.

steps.title: Reconciliation finds what slipped
steps.body: Even good code loses events: a webhook dropped after retries, a bug, a manual refund at the PSP. So each day the worker downloads the PSP's settlement report and compares it line by line with our ledger. Here the PSP lists a 50.00 refund our ledger never saw, leaving a gap of 5,000 cents. Bank statements get the same check. The worker raises a "break" for people to investigate instead of silently fixing it.
steps.idea: Reconciliation is the independent audit that catches errors the real-time path cannot see.
steps.caption: The daily report versus the ledger exposes a 50.00 mismatch.

steps.title: Exactly-once is a promise we build
steps.body: No network gives true exactly-once delivery. What we build is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent handlers, which has the same effect. The remaining gap is closed with a compensating ledger entry that books the missing refund, never by editing history. Rules of thumb: keep idempotency keys at least 24 hours (longer than clients retry, and resolve UNKNOWN payments before the PSP's own key expires); keep ledger rows for the legal retention period, often years. Store money as whole numbers in cents, never as floats.
steps.idea: Effectively-once = retries + idempotency + append-only corrections. Never edit the past; add to it.
steps.caption: A compensating entry books the refund and the gap closes.

steps.title: Four layers of safety
steps.body: Four layers of safety. Idempotency keys make client retries safe. A PENDING, UNKNOWN, CAPTURED state machine makes timeouts safe. The double-entry, append-only ledger makes the books check themselves. Deduplicated webhooks and daily reconciliation catch whatever still slips through. Each layer assumes the one before it will sometimes fail, and that mindset is the whole design.
steps.idea: Assume every step can repeat or fail; build each layer so repeating it changes nothing.
steps.caption: Safe retries, balanced books, and an independent audit.

quiz.q: A client sends POST /payments with key K and the connection drops before any response. It retries with key K. What should the API do if the first attempt already succeeded?
options: Process it again, because the first response was never seen
Return the stored result of the first attempt without charging again
Reject the retry with an error because the key is already used
Delete the key and start fresh so the data is clean
quiz.why: The key exists so a retry is a replay. The API returns the saved outcome, so the card is charged once and the client still learns the result.

quiz.q: The PSP call times out after 10 seconds. What is the correct payment state?
options: FAILED, so the customer can try again immediately
SUCCEEDED, since most calls succeed
UNKNOWN until resolved by a retry with the same key, a status lookup or a webhook
CANCELLED and refunded automatically
quiz.why: A timeout does not tell you whether the card was charged. Marking it failed risks a double charge on retry; marking it success risks shipping unpaid goods. Resolve it by asking.

quiz.q: Why is a payment ledger append-only with balanced debit and credit rows?
options: It uses less disk space than updating rows
It lets the database skip transactions
It removes the need for reconciliation
Corrections are new opposite entries, so history is auditable and total debits always equal credits
quiz.why: Never editing rows preserves the audit trail, and balanced transactions make any bug show up as a nonzero sum. It does not replace reconciliation, which compares against outside parties.

quiz.q: The same payment.succeeded webhook arrives three times. Which design handles it correctly?
options: Store the event id with a unique constraint and ignore repeats, also checking the payment's current state
Trust the PSP to send each event exactly once, so no extra checks are needed
Apply the event every time it arrives so that no retry is ever lost
Drop all webhooks and rely only on the synchronous API response instead
quiz.why: Webhook delivery is at-least-once and can be reordered. Dedup by event id plus state checks makes repeated delivery harmless, and you still keep webhooks because they report later changes.

quiz.q: Every webhook we received was processed and every ledger transaction balanced, yet the daily PSP report shows a refund our ledger lacks. What does this show?
options: Reconciliation duplicates the webhook checks and can be removed to save cost
The ledger must be edited in place so that it matches the PSP report again
The idempotency store is corrupted and every stored key must be purged
Internal consistency does not prove agreement with the outside world, so you need the independent comparison
quiz.why: A ledger can balance perfectly and still be wrong about reality, for example a missed event. Reconciliation against the PSP and bank is the check that finds it, fixed with a compensating entry.

cheatsheet.def: Client-chosen unique id per purchase intent, sent on every retry. The server claims it with a unique insert and replays the saved result.
Fingerprint of the body saved with the key. Same key with a different body is a client error, not a replay.
Result of a timeout after a side effect may have happened. Resolve by retry with the same key, status query or webhook; never guess.
Append-only rows where every transaction has debits equal to credits. Total debits minus total credits is always zero; fix errors with new entries.
Store money as integers (cents) with a currency code. Floats cause rounding drift.
Unique constraint on the provider event id, stored in the same transaction as the state change, plus state checks, so duplicates and reordering are harmless.
Daily comparison of ledger with PSP and bank reports. Differences become breaks that are investigated; true ledger gaps are fixed with new adjusting entries.
At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. True exactly-once delivery is not available over a network.

lab.prompt: Design the backend for a payments product handling 10 million card payments per day. Cover the idempotent payment API, the state machine, the ledger schema, PSP integration, webhook handling and reconciliation. Show how a double charge is prevented when the client retries after a timeout.
requirements: Compute average and peak payments per second, stating your peak factor
Specify the idempotency key flow: where it is stored, uniqueness, request hash, and retention period
Define the payment states and the transitions allowed, including UNKNOWN
Sketch the ledger tables and show one payment and one refund as balanced entries in integer minor units
Explain how you call the PSP safely, including its idempotency key and timeouts
Describe webhook ingestion: ack quickly, dedup by event id, handle out-of-order events
Describe the reconciliation job, what a break is, and how you correct it without editing history
hints: 10M per day divided by 86,400 seconds is about 115 per second; with a peak factor of 10 that is roughly 1,200 per second. One well-provisioned primary can handle that; shard by merchant only for headroom.
Use a relational database with ACID transactions for the ledger and payments; write the payment row and ledger rows in one transaction.
A UNIQUE(merchant_id, idempotency_key) constraint is the simplest correct claim mechanism; a Redis lock alone can lose state.
Derive the PSP idempotency key from your payment id so every retry of the same payment hits the same provider key.
Keep a stuck-payment sweeper that queries the PSP for payments in UNKNOWN for longer than a few minutes.
Reconciliation should compare three sources: PSP report, bank settlement and your ledger, matching on the provider reference.
checklist: Retrying with the same key can never create a second charge
A timeout after the PSP call leaves the payment in UNKNOWN, not FAILED
Every ledger transaction sums to zero and no row is updated or deleted
Duplicate and out-of-order webhooks are harmless
Money is stored as integers with a currency
Reconciliation runs daily and corrections are compensating entries
